analysis.one_liner: Requires a licensed physician to personally review and sign off on any Medicare Advantage denial made with AI.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on July 16, 2026 and sent to two House committees, and has seen no action since; it has one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare Advantage plans — private insurers that cover about half of Medicare beneficiaries — increasingly use artificial intelligence to help deny requests for prior authorization, the step where an insurer must approve a treatment before the patient can get it. This bill would not ban that technology, but it would stop a plan from issuing a denial based on AI output unless a qualified physician — licensed and board-certified in the relevant specialty — personally reviews and approves it, signs an attestation that the judgment was independent of the AI, and makes themselves available to the treating doctor. Plans would also have to disclose AI's role to patients, keep denial records for 10 years, report their AI-based denials to federal regulators every 90 days, and submit to government audits of the algorithms.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Advantage enrollees whose needed care — hospital stays, post-acute care, scans, treatments — is at risk of being denied by an algorithm rather than by a doctor exercising individual judgment. Their treating physicians also gain: they would get the reviewer's attestation, a direct line to the physician reviewer, and a documented individualized basis for any denial.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare Advantage enrollees facing care denials

how_it_helps.text: An MA plan may not deny prior authorization based on AI output unless a qualified physician reviewer, practicing under the plan's medical director, reviews and approves the denial and signs an attestation that the medical judgment was independent of the AI and that any software used was administrative only [S2].

Plans must give the requesting provider a copy of that attestation, a chance to communicate directly with the physician reviewer, and an opportunity to discuss the individualized clinical basis for the denial before it is finalized [S2].

Plans must disclose to patients and providers that AI was used in the denial, give the physician reviewer's National Provider Identifier, and keep denial records — including attestations and AI documentation — for at least 10 years [S2].

Plans must report their AI-based prior authorization denials to the Secretary of Health and Human Services every 90 days, including the signed attestations and the algorithms and decision protocols behind them, and the Secretary gains authority to audit the plans' AI use, compare AI outputs to actual denials, and interview employees [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers would bear the cost of staffing physician reviews for AI-assisted denials, the recordkeeping, the quarterly reporting, and audit exposure. Health insurers are paid fixed monthly premiums per enrollee by Medicare, so those costs come out of their margins or get baked into the bids they submit for future years — a portion could eventually surface in higher plan premiums or richer-denial economics. The AI-denial software industry would also lose a market niche.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare Advantage insurers and denial-software vendors

drawbacks.text: The bill only polices denials that involve AI; it does nothing to limit how often plans require prior authorization in the first place or how many requests are denied overall, so a plan could simply route denials through human staff and continue the same volume [S2].

The core protection is a signed attestation that the reviewer exercised independent judgment, which depends on reviewers answering honestly — the enforcement backstop is audits and reporting, not an automatic penalty for a false attestation [S2].

Requiring a board-certified physician in the relevant specialty to personally review and approve every AI-touched denial adds administrative and staffing cost to plans, which insurers can be expected to pass into their Medicare bids, and the bill requires the Secretary to issue a final rule within one year of enactment, adding a compliance build-out before benefits arrive [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: it targets the specific practice of letting an algorithm effectively decide whether a patient gets care, and puts a named, licensed physician on the hook for each such denial. The costs are administrative and fall on insurers, some of which would likely flow into premiums. The design has gaps — it leaves the prior-authorization system itself intact and leans on attestations rather than penalties — but as a backstop against fully automated care denials it is a reasonable trade.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, and neither has taken it up yet; with Congress still in session, it is waiting on a committee that has shown no interest.

narrative.text: Rep. Conaway introduced the bill in the House on July 16, 2026, with Rep. Murphy as the cosponsor [S1] [S2].

The Speaker's referral sent the bill to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which splits jurisdiction over Medicare Advantage between the two panels [S4].
Since introduction, the only action on the bill is the referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers benefit from the inaction: the current system, in which AI-assisted denials require no individual physician sign-off, disclosure, or algorithm audit, remains in place as long as the bill sits in committee. Enrollees who are denied care are no worse off than before, but they gain nothing yet either.

for.name: Rep. Herb Conaway
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce member (D-NJ)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it through the House; a physician by background sponsoring restrictions on AI-driven coverage denials.

for.name: Rep. Murphy
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a Republican as well as a Democratic sponsor.

against.name: Medicare Advantage insurance industry
against.role: Insurers whose denial workflow the bill would constrain
against.what_they_did: Has not acted on this bill, but the industry's business depends heavily on prior-authorization controls and has historically opposed tighter restrictions on denial practices.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is sponsored by a Democrat and cosponsored by one Republican; no committee or floor votes have occurred yet, so the partisan shape beyond the two sponsors is unknown.

industries.note: Insurers' prior-authorization denials — including AI-assisted ones — reduce what they pay for care while collecting fixed premiums, so every averted denial is money kept. The bill forces a qualified physician to take individual responsibility for each AI-based denial, adds disclosure, 10-year records, quarterly federal reporting, and audit exposure, directly shrinking the margin that automated denials produce.

industries.industry: Health-care AI and denial-management software vendors
industries.note: Firms selling AI tools that generate coverage denials for insurers lose part of their value proposition: the bill requires the algorithms and decision protocols behind denials to be reported to regulators and lets the Secretary compare AI outputs to actual denials and audit the systems. Software used only for administrative purposes remains allowed.

The bill creates a required role — a licensed, board-certified physician reviewer with direct patient-side accountability for each denial — and gives treating physicians a channel to reach that reviewer before a denial is finalized. This pushes coverage decisions back toward human medical judgment, which physicians have long argued AI tools undermine.

analysis.trajectory: A bill referred to two committees with a single cosponsor and no action since introduction rarely advances: without a subcommittee hearing, a full-committee markup, and a floor slot, the likely path is that it sits in committee and dies when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce both share jurisdiction over Medicare, which makes it easy for the bill to stall between them.
